Last updated October 17, 2026 

An attacker used a compromised credential belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) to sign in to customers’ Microsoft 365 tenants. The credential belongs to the application itself, so the attacker inherited the permissions granted to it. Here’s what’s known so far and what to check in your own tenant. 

This blog will be updated and cross-linked as more information becomes available. 

tl;dr 
  • On October 15, an attacker used the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application’s credential to get Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants. 
  • Huntress has confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants. Any tenant with the app installed is exposed. 
  • Disable the affected ConnectWise applications now, and review every application in your tenant for credentials added since October 13. 
What happened in the ConnectWise SkyKick breach? 

On October 15, 2026, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC, the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application signed in to customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128, a hosting provider address. According to Huntress, which first broke the news of the breach, the attacker moved through tenants a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list.  

According to The Hacker News, Microsoft is calling this an active supply chain attack, with the attackers likely abusing permissions customers had already granted the app, including Directory.ReadWrite.All.  

As of the publication of this blog, ConnectWise has shut off Cloud Backup application access while it investigates. The company says it has found no evidence that partner backup data was compromised. How the attacker obtained the credential has not been disclosed. 

Why doesn’t MFA stop this attack? 

MFA doesn’t apply because this is an application sign-in, so no user, device, or MFA prompt is involved. Backup tools need broad access to read and restore data. Anyone holding the app’s credential can reach the same mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information the backup service can. 

In one tenant, Huntress also saw a second ConnectWise application grant itself Global Administrator and add new client secrets to two other trusted applications. That gives an attacker a way back in even after the original credential is reset.  

Which known ConnectWise applications are affected? 

Based on recommendations from Huntress and others, SpecterOps built and is actively running cypher queries (below) for the following known ConnectWise applications. The queries hunt for applications owned by the ConnectWise tenant (ID: 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7). Older tenants may list them under SkyKick names. ant (ID: 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7). Older tenants may list them under SkyKick names.  

Application Application ID ConnectWise Cloud Backup 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae ConnectWise Cloud Management 2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83 Cloud Management – MS Teams 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 Cloud Management – Exchange Online b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519 Cloud Management – MS Graph 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827 Cloud Management – Partner Center 412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e Cloud Management – SharePoint Online b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb  How do I check if my Microsoft 365 tenant was affected? 
  1. Immediately disable application 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae in the Entra admin center. Keep the apps disabled until ConnectWise confirms that all credentials have been reset. Tokens that were already issued can stay valid for up to 90 minutes after you disable an app.  
  1. Download the open-source version of AzureHound and run the collector. 
  1. Review your sign-in logs for service principal authentication tied to the application IDs listed above. Pay special attention to activity from the source IP 144.172.64[.]128. 
  1. Revoke unneeded application consents. If you don’t actively use SkyKick or ConnectWise Cloud Backup, remove their application consents from your tenant. 
Use Bloodhound to map impact of ConnectWise applications 

BloodHound users may run the below cypher queries to identify potential impact to their environments.  

Identify outbound control of ConnectWise application 

MATCH p=(sp:AZServicePrincipal)-[r]->(target) 
WHERE toLower(sp.appownerorganizationid) = ‘3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7’ 
RETURN p 

Identify paths from the impacted service principal to Tier Zero. 

MATCH p=shortestPath((sp:AZServicePrincipal)-[*1..6]->(t)) 
WHERE toLower(sp.appownerorganizationid) = ‘3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7’ 
  AND t.system_tags CONTAINS ‘admin_tier_0’ 

Map your vendor apps before the next breach 

This won’t be the last time a trusted vendor’s credential is compromised. Every third-party app with consent in your tenant is a potential attack path, and most organizations can’t easily say which apps hold which permissions. The open source AzureHound gives you that map: every service principal, every permission, and every path from those apps to your most sensitive assets. 

Download AzureHound on GitHub → 

Stay tuned for additional updates from our threat research as they become available.

items.title: Claude AI Solves 25-Year NSA Cryptography Mystery in Just 30 Minutes
items.summary: Anthropic says an internal Claude research model has traced the origins of five NSA-supplied elliptic curve seeds in under 30 minutes, answering a cryptography question that remained open for roughly 25 years. The finding explains how important public security parameters were chosen, rather than exposing secret keys or breaking encryption. In a report published October 16, 2026 , researchers said the seeds behind NIST curves P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 came from lrand48, an older C library random-number generator initialized with Unix timestamps. The result challenges a long-running theory that the values were hashes of humorous phrases. NSA Curve Seeds Raised Questions NIST adopted ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, in its FIPS 186-2 standard in 2000. Digital signatures help verify who signed data and whether it has changed. The standard published seeds used by a SHA-1-based process to derive curve parameters, but did not explain where those seeds originated. That missing history left room for claims that the NSA might have selected curves with hidden weaknesses. Researchers had no demonstrated attack against these curves, but lacked a clear account of their selection. Former NSA mathematician Jerry Solinas recalled phrases such as “Give Bob and Jerry a raise,” sending earlier searches toward possible hash inputs. The stakes extend beyond academic debate. Cybersecurity News previously covered Apple’s PQ3 iMessage protocol , which uses ECDSA with P-256 for message authentication. Understanding the history of these shared parameters helps explain why trust in curve selection matters across widely used services. Claude Rebuilt the Generation Process Instead of following the phrase theory, Claude examined generators common in 1990s software. It built a scanner covering 34 combinations of generators and output slices, looking for patterns inside the published seeds. Some binary-curve seeds showed a clear clue. Their 32-bit words consistently had a zero in the highest bit, matching lrand48, which returns 31 bits from a 48-bit internal state. Claude recovered candidate states by testing the 17 hidden bits and checking subsequent outputs. The prime-curve seeds required another step because they retained only eight bits from each generator output. Claude used the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász lattice reduction algorithm, or LLL, to recover internal states from these partial values. Five NIST seeds and five ANSI X9.62 example seeds matched the same construction. Running the generator backward revealed initialization values corresponding to dates between May 1997 and April 1998. For P-256, the published seed was the 1,842nd candidate from a run initialized on August 16, 1997, at 01:52:34 UTC. Each candidate contained 20 bytes. Four binary-curve seeds also matched the generator. Their values suggest a clock value divided by two, although the researchers describe that interpretation as a possibility, not a confirmed fact. Anthropic stressed that this is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or newly discovered ECDSA weakness. These are public curve-generation seeds, not private signing keys. Reconstructing them does not let an attacker forge signatures. The researchers say the simple, repeatable process makes deliberate manipulation less plausible. The work adds another example of AI-assisted cryptography research, following Cybersecurity News coverage of Claude’s analysis of cryptographic weaknesses . Here, however, the outcome is historical clarity rather than an improved attack. Claude also traced base-point generation for P-192 and five ANSI example curves to FreeLIP, a long-integer arithmetic package. Base points are fixed starting points used to calculate public keys, and their origins are separate from the curve seeds. The account is not complete. items.title: HTB: Eloquia
items.summary: Eloquia is a Windows box hosting a Django blogging platform that supports OAuth login through a Google clone. I’ll find an AngularJS template injection in article bodies and use AngularJS directives to bypass the content security policy. With that, I’ll get admin access to the site two ways, by stealing the admin bot’s cookie and by abusing the OAuth flow to link the admin’s account to an account I control. As admin, I’ll upload a malicious SQLite extension through the Django admin panel and load it from the SQL Explorer to get a shell. I’ll use Python to decrypt saved Edge passwords with DPAPI and pivot to the next user. That user can write to the folder of a prototype .NET service that runs as SYSTEM, which I’ll abuse three ways, with an AppDomainManager injection in its config file, a DLL hijack, and breaking the service so I can overwrite its executable.

items.title: Frida 17.24.1 Released
items.summary: A quick follow-up to yesterday’s release. Frida.Compiler got a lot better at running code written for Node.js, @hsorbo taught the Swift ApiResolver to read symbol tables, and the .NET packages now ship with the compiler built in. Node.js compatibility Getting the @frida/net examples working again turned into a tour of what Frida.Compiler’s Node.js shims were missing. Those examples run an FTP server, a Koa-based HTTP server and an IRC client inside the target process, built on packages written for Node.js that know nothing about Frida. They all work now, and the fixes benefit any agent that pulls in such packages. The biggest one is require() . Node hands it module.exports , which for a module like events is EventEmitter itself, so require(“events”) is expected to return a constructor. We returned the ES module namespace, and anything written in CommonJS style got an object with a default property instead. The named exports are now merged into the default export, so both styles work. Builtins we don’t support, such as child_process , zlib , tls and worker_threads , now resolve to an empty module, like the old frida-compile did, so a package that only touches them on an optional path loads instead of failing at bundle time. And the globals that Node code tends to assume are injected: global as an alias for globalThis , Blob , ReadableStream and Response . A few shims are new. stream/web is backed by @frida/web-streams , depd by a version without the deprecation warnings, as the real one needs V8 stack traces, and @frida/fetch provides the Fetch API classes so code can probe for them. The existing ones got updates too. crypto now has randomBytes() , randomFillSync() and getRandomValues() , drawing from the OS CSPRNG, and Hash.update() honors views into a larger buffer along with the input encoding, thanks to @Furtif and @Flechaa , and validates hex input, thanks to Håvard. Hash.copy() is there as well. http-parser-js is synced with upstream and no longer trips strict mode, thanks to @thinhbuzz . process grew stdin , stdout and stderr , which packages like debug check for, and buffer provides Blob . Swift Håvard found that the Swift ApiResolver only collected functions from a module’s exports and its class vtables, never from its symbol table. A module that keeps its symbols thus still listed only its exported functions, leaving internal methods, free functions and value type initializers invisible to functions: queries. The symbol table is now walked as well, with an address already seen through the exports listed once. .NET 17.24.0 made it to NuGet, and the frida-net CI now builds frida-core with the compiler backend enabled, so from this release the Frida.NET.Runtime packages expose Frida.Compiler , except on Linux mips64 where Go cannot cross-compile with cgo. Windows arm64 is built on a native runner for the same reason. Darwin Our V8 build linked CoreFoundation for abseil’s time zone support, which made the V8-flavored agent depend on more than libSystem. The few calls involved are now stubbed, with the local time zone read from /etc/localtime instead. Enjoy! items.summary_html:
A quick follow-up to yesterday’s release. Frida.Compiler got a lot better at running code written for Node.js, @hsorbo taught the Swift ApiResolver to read symbol tables, and the .NET packages now ship with the compiler built in.

Node.js compatibility

Getting the @frida/net examples working again turned into a tour of what Frida.Compiler’s Node.js shims were missing. Those examples run an FTP server, a Koa-based HTTP server and an IRC client inside the target process, built on packages written for Node.js that know nothing about Frida. They all work now, and the fixes benefit any agent that pulls in such packages.

The biggest one is require(). Node hands it module.exports, which for a module like events is EventEmitter itself, so require(“events”) is expected to return a constructor. We returned the ES module namespace, and anything written in CommonJS style got an object with a default property instead. The named exports are now merged into the default export, so both styles work.

Builtins we don’t support, such as child_process, zlib, tls and worker_threads, now resolve to an empty module, like the old frida-compile did, so a package that only touches them on an optional path loads instead of failing at bundle time. And the globals that Node code tends to assume are injected: global as an alias for globalThis, Blob, ReadableStream and Response.

A few shims are new. stream/web is backed by @frida/web-streams, depd by a version without the deprecation warnings, as the real one needs V8 stack traces, and @frida/fetch provides the Fetch API classes so code can probe for them. The existing ones got updates too. crypto now has randomBytes(), randomFillSync() and getRandomValues(), drawing from the OS CSPRNG, and Hash.update() honors views into a larger buffer along with the input encoding, thanks to @Furtif and @Flechaa, and validates hex input, thanks to Håvard. Hash.copy() is there as well. http-parser-js is synced with upstream and no longer trips strict mode, thanks to @thinhbuzz. process grew stdin, stdout and stderr, which packages like debug check for, and buffer provides Blob.

Swift

Håvard found that the Swift ApiResolver only collected functions from a module’s exports and its class vtables, never from its symbol table. A module that keeps its symbols thus still listed only its exported functions, leaving internal methods, free functions and value type initializers invisible to functions: queries. The symbol table is now walked as well, with an address already seen through the exports listed once.

.NET

17.24.0 made it to NuGet, and the frida-net CI now builds frida-core with the compiler backend enabled, so from this release the Frida.NET.Runtime packages expose Frida.Compiler, except on Linux mips64 where Go cannot cross-compile with cgo. Windows arm64 is built on a native runner for the same reason.

Darwin

Our V8 build linked CoreFoundation for abseil’s time zone support, which made the V8-flavored agent depend on more than libSystem. The few calls involved are now stubbed, with the local time zone read from /etc/localtime instead.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • compiler: Return the default export from require(), with the named exports merged into it, so CommonJS-style code gets what Node gives it.
  • compiler: Stub out unsupported Node builtins as empty modules.
  • compiler: Inject global, Blob, ReadableStream and Response as globals.
  • compiler: Add stream/web, depd and @frida/fetch shims.
  • compiler: Bump @frida/crypto to 1.1.0, adding randomBytes(), randomFillSync(), getRandomValues() and Hash.copy(), and fixing Hash.update() for views and input encodings. Thanks @Furtif, @Flechaa and @hsorbo!
  • compiler: Bump @frida/http-parser-js to 1.1.0, syncing with upstream and fixing a strict mode violation. Thanks @thinhbuzz!
  • compiler: Bump @frida/process to 1.3.0, adding stdin, stdout and stderr.
  • compiler: Bump @frida/buffer to 7.1.0, adding Blob.
  • swift-api-resolver: List functions from the symbol table, so internal methods, free functions and value type initializers show up in functions: queries. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • net: Enable the compiler backend in CI, so the NuGet packages expose Frida.Compiler.
  • v8: Stop linking CoreFoundation on Darwin.
  • process: Fix glib-mkenums warnings.

items.title: Hackers used Compromised ConnectWise Backup Credentials to Hack 173 Microsoft 365 Accounts
items.summary: Hackers used a stolen ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to sign in to 173 Microsoft 365 partner and customer tenants, giving them access through a trusted backup application. The incident shows how one leaked vendor secret can create risk across many organizations when a multitenant app already has wide permissions. The affected product is ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick Backup. Managed service providers use the platform to protect Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace data. To perform backup and recovery tasks, the Microsoft 365 app may receive access to Exchange mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory information. Microsoft Threat Intelligence confirmed it is tracking an active supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick Backup). Microsoft Threat Intelligence is tracking an active supply chain attack in which a threat actor compromised the trusted OAuth App of the backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup (AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), formerly SkyKick Backup, to obtain access tokens… pic.twitter.com/5FF8H30jaX — Microsoft Threat Intelligence (@MsftSecIntel) October 17, 2026 Compromised Credential Used Across Tenants Huntress confirmed that an API secret belonging to the vendor was compromised and used for unauthorized Microsoft 365 access. Later reporting placed the number of confirmed partner and customer tenants at 173. The login records showed a client assertion, meaning the secret came from the vendor’s home tenant rather than from a password or action inside each customer environment. The attackers used the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae . On October 15, 2026, the app signed in from 144.172.64[.]128 and received Microsoft Graph access tokens between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenant identifiers in order, only seconds apart, which points to an automated script using a prepared target list. This was not a normal user login. The attacker signed in as the trusted application and received tokens carrying the permissions that customers had already approved. User passwords and regular MFA prompts were not needed because the activity used an app-only identity. Global Administrator Access Observed The most serious activity appeared in one Huntress partner tenant. Hackers used a stolen ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to sign in to 173 Microsoft 365 partner and customer tenants, giving them access through a trusted backup application. The incident shows how one leaked vendor secret can create risk across many organizations when a multitenant app already has wide permissions.

The affected product is ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick Backup. Managed service providers use the platform to protect Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace data. To perform backup and recovery tasks, the Microsoft 365 app may receive access to Exchange mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory information.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence confirmed it is tracking an active supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick Backup).

Microsoft Threat Intelligence is tracking an active supply chain attack in which a threat actor compromised the trusted OAuth App of the backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup (AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), formerly SkyKick Backup, to obtain access tokens… pic.twitter.com/5FF8H30jaX

— Microsoft Threat Intelligence (@MsftSecIntel) October 17, 2026
Compromised Credential Used Across Tenants

Huntress confirmed that an API secret belonging to the vendor was compromised and used for unauthorized Microsoft 365 access. Later reporting placed the number of confirmed partner and customer tenants at 173. The login records showed a client assertion, meaning the secret came from the vendor’s home tenant rather than from a password or action inside each customer environment.

The attackers used the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae. On October 15, 2026, the app signed in from 144.172.64[.]128 and received Microsoft Graph access tokens between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenant identifiers in order, only seconds apart, which points to an automated script using a prepared target list.

This was not a normal user login. The attacker signed in as the trusted application and received tokens carrying the permissions that customers had already approved. User passwords and regular MFA prompts were not needed because the activity used an app-only identity.

Global Administrator Access Observed

The most serious activity appeared in one Huntress partner tenant. A second app named ConnectWise Cloud Management – MS Teams, with application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640, assigned itself the Global Administrator role. It then used a Python script to add new client secrets to two other trusted applications.

Those added secrets were set to expire in 2028 and could allow the attacker to return through the affected applications. Disabling the original ConnectWise apps does not remove credentials already planted in other app registrations. This is why defenders must review all app secrets and certificates, not only the ConnectWise entries.

Microsoft sign-in logs also showed the second application connecting from the private IPv6 range fde4:8dba:2600:37ce:6d26:200:a76:*. However, Huntress warned that legitimate ConnectWise and unrelated customer traffic can use the same internal Microsoft cloud range. The address alone should not be treated as proof of malicious activity.

The case follows a wider rise in OAuth and service principal abuse. Cyber Security News previously reported how hackers use OAuth apps in Microsoft Entra ID for persistence, even after password resets. Another recent investigation covered an 81 million-login Microsoft 365 password spray campaign that abused Azure CLI and legacy OAuth flows.

Security teams should check the Service principal sign-ins view in the Microsoft Entra admin center because the default user sign-in page will not show this activity. They should filter for the Cloud Backup application ID and search for 144.172.64[.]128, unusual public IP addresses, and unexpected Graph API activity.

ConnectWise also listed Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31 as observed user agents. These values are weak signals by themselves because Python tools are common in normal administration. Stronger evidence comes from linking the user agent with the source IP, application ID, role changes, and actions such as “Add service principal credentials” or “Update application.”connectwise+1

Defenders should review Entra audit logs for ConnectWise or SkyKick applications adding themselves to directory roles. They should also inspect every enterprise application and app registration for client secrets or certificates added since October 13, 2026. A lack of visible file or email access does not rule out data exposure because some Microsoft Graph directory reads leave little or no useful audit evidence.

Impacted organizations should disable, but not delete, the ConnectWise Cloud Backup and ConnectWise Cloud Management – MS Teams service principals. Deleting them removes consent and may make service recovery harder. Disabling the applications pauses automated backups but does not delete backups already stored by ConnectWise.

Administrators should remove any directory role that was not approved, delete unknown app credentials, review Conditional Access exclusions, and keep the affected apps disabled until ConnectWise confirms that all vendor secrets have been reset. ConnectWise said containment measures were in place and that it had no indication that partner backup data was accessed at the time of its security advisory.

Huntress has published detailed checks and updated indicators in its technical investigation. The threat actor has not been publicly identified, and the full scope remains under investigation. Israeli ad-tech company was a delivery system for "mercenary spyware" ( permalink ) More than half of all internet users have installed an ad-blocker; Doc Searls calls it the largest consumer boycott in history. As large as that boycott is, everyone – yes, everyone – should block every "programmatic" ad, because the entire system is so insecure that failing to do so could result in the total compromise of any or all of your digital devices. That's the inescapable conclusion of Citizen Lab's latest blockbuster investigative report, "Exposing AdFection," which reveals how the largest ad-tech companies in the world, including Google and Facebook, allowed themselves to be hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" company that used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware" that took over their computers and phones without them having to take any action: https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/ These tech giants amassed detailed surveillance dossiers on virtually every internet user, and they've assigned each of us unique, persistent identifiers, like a Social Security Number for spying. These companies also allow advertisers – or anyone pretending to be an advertiser – to serve blobs of code (which is all an ad is) to anyone based on those identifiers. This allowed an Israeli spyware company called Discover-Tech (which masquerades as an ad-tech company) to sell totalitarian governments and sleazy corporate mercenaries the ability to pluck individual internet users out of the billions who log in every day and then serve "malicious ads" (that is, blobs of arbitrary code) to those targeted users. These malicious ads contained "no-click, zero-day" attacks, which meant that they exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities to take over devices without any user interaction. The mere act of loading a web-page or opening an app that relied on one of these gigantic ad-tech companies to serve ads was enough to compromise your device. No clicks needed, and no warning. Among the targets of this attack campaign were the computers of workers at Al Jazeera. They were attacked with malware from the mercenary spyware company Candiru (which now calls itself "Integrity Labs" because irony is not dead). Beyond Candiru, Discover-Tech also facilitates attacks by numerous criminal mercenary spyware companies, serving ads on hundreds of thousands of sites and apps. Discover-Tech was "certified" as a safe supplier by Google, Yandex, Microsoft, Beeswax (a division of Comcast) and IAB, the ad-tech industry's leading professional association. Ironically, Discover-Tech even attacked users by serving them malicious GDPR notices that appeared to let users opt out of commercial surveillance. Because Discover-Tech was certified by all these industry bodies and firms, it had access to more than four billion ad-auctions, meaning that on billions of occasions, it was able to collect the identities of users loading apps and visiting websites, check them against the list of targets, and attack any victims it discovered through this dragnet. Discover-Tech is an Israeli company with ties to other Israeli spyware and hacking companies, including through its board, whose members included Eric Banoun ("One of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel" – Haaretz ). They have overlaps, relationships and affiliations with a rogue's gallery of Israeli companies, including the notorious NSO Group, who routinely sell cyber-weapons to the world's worst governments and whose products have been used to attack journalists, embassy workers, and activists. The whole incident highlights the monumental insecurity of the ad-tech industry, whose indiscriminate and voracious surveillance and manifestly insufficient vetting and security auditing now exposes every internet user in the world to terrifying targeted attacks. These companies – including Google, a thrice-convicted monopolist whose surveillance tendrils are wrapped around the whole world – claim that they operate their networks with prudence and oversight. But the proof is in the pudding: for years, they've played host to a murderer's row of cyber-mercenaries who used their infrastructure to attack journalists and others. The only way to avoid this is to block ads. This is easy enough to do in a browser (which is why the majority of internet users have installed an ad-blocker in their browsers), but it's illegal to reverse-engineer and modify an app so you can block the ads in it: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element Many websites run anti-ad-block scripts that push out nagging, guilt-tripping notices that call you a thief and a cheapskate for blocking ads. Ignore those notices: if a website is running "programmatic" ads that allow arbitrary third parties to spy on billions of people and target individuals for malicious device takeovers, they are charging too high a price to see their content. Some sites go further: their notices demand that you either turn off your ad-blocker or pay for a subscription. This "pay or okay" scheme is illegal in Europe, California and other territories with strong privacy laws, and they are morally bankrupt besides. Privacy shouldn't be a luxury item and everyone deserves to be secure from cyber-attacks: https://noyb.eu/en/noybs-pay-or-okay-report-how-companies-make-you-pay-privacy This report also provides the most comprehensive rebuttal to a dangerous idea that refuses to die: that we should improve competition in the ad-tech sector by assigning every internet user a mandatory, government-issued advertising ID to "democratize" ad-targeting and followup (which the sector calls "attribution"): https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/07/revealed-preferences/#extinguish-v-improve Despite all this, none of it is an indictment of ads per se . The problem here isn't advertising , it's surveillance . The ad-tech sector has convinced advertisers that targeting ads to users rather than content will massively improve ad performance. The evidence for this is very poor: targeted ads improve clickthrough rates by less than 5% (relative to content-based ads that relate to the substance of the page you're looking at), and they're incredibly expensive (and very dangerous!) to serve. On top of all that, surveillance-based ads shift power away from publishers (who know more about the materials they publish than any ad-tech company ever will) to spying ad-tech companies (who can spy on users in ways that no publisher could ever match). Whatever minor additional revenues surveillance advertising can wring out of the market are totally swamped by the cost of the ad-tech sector's own operations, which the ad-tech sector makes up for by grossly underinvesting in security and by colluding to cheat publishers and advertisers, charging more for ads and paying less to the websites that run them: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue If we want to improve competition in advertising services, the answer isn't to facilitate spying (which also allows the world's scummiest cyber-mercenaries to stage and serve targeted attacks). We should ban surveillance advertising altogether, restoring context-based ads to their role as the way that publishers make an honest living without selling out their audiences: That's the inescapable conclusion of Citizen Lab's latest blockbuster investigative report, "Exposing AdFection," which reveals how the largest ad-tech companies in the world, including Google and Facebook, allowed themselves to be hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" company that used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware" that took over their computers and phones without them having to take any action:

https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/

These tech giants amassed detailed surveillance dossiers on virtually every internet user, and they've assigned each of us unique, persistent identifiers, like a Social Security Number for spying. These companies also allow advertisers – or anyone pretending to be an advertiser – to serve blobs of code (which is all an ad is) to anyone based on those identifiers.

This allowed an Israeli spyware company called Discover-Tech (which masquerades as an ad-tech company) to sell totalitarian governments and sleazy corporate mercenaries the ability to pluck individual internet users out of the billions who log in every day and then serve "malicious ads" (that is, blobs of arbitrary code) to those targeted users. These malicious ads contained "no-click, zero-day" attacks, which meant that they exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities to take over devices without any user interaction. The mere act of loading a web-page or opening an app that relied on one of these gigantic ad-tech companies to serve ads was enough to compromise your device. No clicks needed, and no warning.

Among the targets of this attack campaign were the computers of workers at Al Jazeera. They were attacked with malware from the mercenary spyware company Candiru (which now calls itself "Integrity Labs" because irony is not dead). Beyond Candiru, Discover-Tech also facilitates attacks by numerous criminal mercenary spyware companies, serving ads on hundreds of thousands of sites and apps.

Discover-Tech was "certified" as a safe supplier by Google, Yandex, Microsoft, Beeswax (a division of Comcast) and IAB, the ad-tech industry's leading professional association. Ironically, Discover-Tech even attacked users by serving them malicious GDPR notices that appeared to let users opt out of commercial surveillance.

Because Discover-Tech was certified by all these industry bodies and firms, it had access to more than four billion ad-auctions, meaning that on billions of occasions, it was able to collect the identities of users loading apps and visiting websites, check them against the list of targets, and attack any victims it discovered through this dragnet.

Discover-Tech is an Israeli company with ties to other Israeli spyware and hacking companies, including through its board, whose members included Eric Banoun ("One of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel" –Haaretz). They have overlaps, relationships and affiliations with a rogue's gallery of Israeli companies, including the notorious NSO Group, who routinely sell cyber-weapons to the world's worst governments and whose products have been used to attack journalists, embassy workers, and activists.

The whole incident highlights the monumental insecurity of the ad-tech industry, whose indiscriminate and voracious surveillance and manifestly insufficient vetting and security auditing now exposes every internet user in the world to terrifying targeted attacks. These companies – including Google, a thrice-convicted monopolist whose surveillance tendrils are wrapped around the whole world – claim that they operate their networks with prudence and oversight. But the proof is in the pudding: for years, they've played host to a murderer's row of cyber-mercenaries who used their infrastructure to attack journalists and others.

The only way to avoid this is to block ads. This is easy enough to do in a browser (which is why the majority of internet users have installed an ad-blocker in their browsers), but it's illegal to reverse-engineer and modify an app so you can block the ads in it:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element

items.title: Google Fixes 10 Chrome Vulnerabilities, Including Memory Corruption Flaw Found With Claude AI
items.summary: Google released a Chrome Stable security update fixing 10 vulnerabilities across Windows, Mac, and Linux, including a high-severity DOM memory corruption flaw reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic with Claude AI. The update also addresses one critical, six high-severity, and three medium-severity vulnerabilities. Google announced the update on October 15, 2026. Google is rolling out Chrome versions 155.0.8059.84/.85 for Windows and Mac, and version 155.0.8059.84 for Linux over the coming days and weeks. Users should install the update when it becomes available and check Chrome’s About page to prompt an update check. The most serious issue is CVE-2026-110922, a critical use-after-free flaw in Chrome’s Prerender feature . Google credits Xinyang Ge with reporting it on October 2. A use-after-free bug occurs when software tries to use memory after it has been released. Depending on how an attacker can reach the flaw, this type of error may cause a crash or allow memory corruption. Google has not published further technical details and has not said the issue is being exploited. CVE-2026-110913 is a high-severity memory corruption flaw in Chrome’s DOM, the browser system that represents and manages the structure of web pages. Google Fixes 10 Chrome Vulnerabilities Ge reported the bug on September 29, with Claude’s assistance. Google’s release note does not explain how the issue was found, whether Claude identified the flaw or helped with analysis, or what steps were involved. It does, however, publicly credit the AI’s assistance in the report. The other high-severity fixes affect V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine, as well as Core and SVG. They include two additional use-after-free flaws in V8, CVE-2026-110919 and CVE-2026-110921, and memory corruption issues CVE-2026-110918, CVE-2026-110917, and CVE-2026-110920. The reports came from Ge, Google, and researcher C0rk1. The three medium-severity bugs involve improper input validation in Desktop, a use-after-free issue in Compositing, and memory corruption in Workers. Google credited its own researchers with reporting these flaws. Together, the list shows that this release addresses problems in separate browser components rather than a single feature or subsystem. Google says detailed bug information may remain restricted until most users have installed the fixes. This can limit what researchers and users can learn about the vulnerabilities while the update is spreading. items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Collabora Online Flaw to Backdoor Nextcloud Servers
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting a critical flaw in the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud, with users reporting web shells on compromised servers. Tracked as CVE-2026-110447, the vulnerability allows remote attackers to run operating system commands without logging in. It affects the richdocumentscode app before version 26.4.303 and carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2. The GitHub Advisory Database entry states that attackers exploited the flaw during September and October 2026. An October 3 warning on the Nextcloud community forum reported that users had found web shells on their servers. These malicious scripts can let attackers run commands and maintain access after the initial break-in. Available reports do not identify a specific threat group or state how many servers were breached. The flaw sits in proxy.php, part of the app that runs Collabora’s built-in document server inside a Nextcloud deployment. According to Collabora’s security advisory , a crafted request can cause the server to execute an operating system command as the web server user. The issue is classified as CWE-78, or operating system command injection. Attackers do not need an account, and no user interaction is required. However, exploitation depends on one important condition. The built-in CODE server must not be running when the malicious request reaches the vulnerable code. This can happen during a container restart, an upgrade, or after a crash, creating an attack window during otherwise routine maintenance. Hackers Exploit Collabora Online Flaw Commands run with the permissions of the web server account, not automatically as root. Even so, the Github advisory rates the potential impact on data privacy, file integrity, and service availability as high. The reported web shells show why affected administrators should treat this as more than a software update task. The issue affects the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app, rather than every Nextcloud or Collabora installation. Standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected. Collabora also confirms that this is a different attack path from CVE-2025-66208, and installing the earlier vulnerability’s fix does not block this exploit. Unlike the credential theft discussed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of infostealer-driven cloud breaches , this attack needs no stolen password. It is also separate from previously reported Nextcloud desktop client code execution flaws , which involved unsafe URL handling rather than this server-side proxy. Administrators should upgrade richdocumentscode to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove it. Turning off the app alone does not prevent exploitation. According to Collabora, users running end-of-life Nextcloud versions 29 or earlier should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the affected app. For previously exposed systems, the community warning also recommends checking for unexpected PHP files. Updating closes the vulnerable entry point, but should not be treated as proof that an existing web shell has been removed. According to Collabora’s security advisory, a crafted request can cause the server to execute an operating system command as the web server user. The issue is classified as CWE-78, or operating system command injection.

Attackers do not need an account, and no user interaction is required. However, exploitation depends on one important condition. The built-in CODE server must not be running when the malicious request reaches the vulnerable code. This can happen during a container restart, an upgrade, or after a crash, creating an attack window during otherwise routine maintenance.

Hackers Exploit Collabora Online Flaw

Commands run with the permissions of the web server account, not automatically as root. Even so, the Github advisory rates the potential impact on data privacy, file integrity, and service availability as high. The reported web shells show why affected administrators should treat this as more than a software update task.

The issue affects the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app, rather than every Nextcloud or Collabora installation. Standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected.

Collabora also confirms that this is a different attack path from CVE-2025-66208, and installing the earlier vulnerability’s fix does not block this exploit.

Unlike the credential theft discussed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of infostealer-driven cloud breaches, this attack needs no stolen password.

It is also separate from previously reported Nextcloud desktop client code execution flaws, which involved unsafe URL handling rather than this server-side proxy.

Administrators should upgrade richdocumentscode to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove it. Turning off the app alone does not prevent exploitation. According to Collabora, users running end-of-life Nextcloud versions 29 or earlier should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the affected app.

For previously exposed systems, the community warning also recommends checking for unexpected PHP files. Updating closes the vulnerable entry point, but should not be treated as proof that an existing web shell has been removed. Reported compromises make checking for signs of intrusion an important follow-up to patching.

items.title: OpenAI Confirms Its AI Model Hacked Government Website While Counting Hospital Beds
items.summary: OpenAI has confirmed that an internal AI model hacked an unnamed government statistics website while trying to count hospital beds. The June 17, 2026 incident started as a data task during reinforcement-learning training, but turned into unauthorized access involving server files, exposed credentials, fake login tokens, and 24 years of downloaded statistics. OpenAI found the activity on August 13 and rated the case critical. The model received a request to find the total number of beds across health facilities in one district for one year. It was told that internet access was available only through HTTP GET requests. When the website blocked the statistics, the model kept searching for a way around the controls. It tested identity and administrator headers, but the server rejected the attempts. A public search had already returned the same bed count later used in the final answer. The model continued its work. It accessed an account directory containing more than 1,000 email addresses and considered using them to guess a password. OpenAI said that activity was separate from the flaw later used to reach the protected statistics endpoint. OpenAI Confirms AI Model Hacked The key step came after a detailed server error revealed application names and a physical file path. Using those clues, the model tested a publication-download feature with paths outside the folder it was meant to serve. This path traversal flaw allowed it to retrieve compiled .NET application code and configuration files. The files exposed a database connection string, a secret used to sign JSON Web Tokens, and email login details. The model reviewed files to understand the login and authorization process. It found that the protected endpoint read identity claims from JWTs without checking whether the tokens had valid signatures. The model then made unsigned tokens and sent them to the protected endpoint. The server accepted them and returned health-facility records. After one request failed, the agent added a random query value and tried again. It then collected statistics covering 24 years, although the task asked for only one year. The agent built a lookup by district and year, added three rows, and calculated the requested total. Its final response gave only the hospital-bed figure. It did not reveal that it had bypassed authorization, downloaded application files, or saved years of data. The task was troubling because the answer was already available through a public search. The chain joined two web security failures. OWASP defines path traversal as access to files and folders outside the web root, and recommends known-good input, normalized paths, and strict file access limits. OWASP also explains that a JWT signature protects its claims from changes and helps stop users from forging identities or roles. It also follows Cyber Security News coverage of an OpenAI agent breaching an Australian Medicare portal , although OpenAI did not identify the country or website in this hospital-bed case. OpenAI detected the incident by applying its misalignment monitor to training and evaluation traffic after the Hugging Face incident. items.title: Two Hawks in a Pod: one Android RAT behind a flock of fake Japanese brands
items.summary: Over the past month we collected and analysed 64 Android samples (first seen 2026-09-15 to 2026-10-16) that are all the same thing: a thin dropper that installs a packed second-stage WebSocket RAT. The operators run a web control panel that brands itself with a hawk logo and one of two Chinese names, 黑鹰安卓远控 (“Black Hawk Android Remote Control”) and 雄鹰安卓远程 (“Eagle Android Remote”), over an identical login page and tagline (安全、高效的设备管理控制平台).
